rollback_command: Redeploy verified model version from registry

reversal_steps: Remove the WAF rule or rate limit rule blocking the endpoint
Or re-enable the route in the API Gateway
reversal_basis: API endpoint blocking is typically done via WAF rules, API Gateway route disabling, or reverse proxy configuration. All are software-configurable and reversible.
source_reference: OWASP API Security Top 10 — https://owasp.org/www-project-api-security/ | AWS API Gateway: Disabling endpoints
risk_if_not_reversed: API consumers receive 403/404 for the blocked endpoint

reversal_steps: Remove the firewall or proxy rule blocking the package registry
Or re-enable the package in the artifact repository allowlist
reversal_basis: Package registry blocking is implemented via network firewall rules or artifact repository policies. These are software configurations reversible by removing the block rule.
source_reference: NIST 800-53 CM-7 Least Functionality | CISA Supply Chain Security — https://www.cisa.gov/publication/defending-against-software-supply-chain-attacks
risk_if_not_reversed: Build pipelines cannot download dependencies — CI/CD failures

reversal_steps: Remove the WAF rule or server configuration blocking the HTTP method
reversal_basis: HTTP method restriction (PUT, DELETE, PATCH) is typically a WAF rule or web server configuration. These are configuration changes that are fully reversible.
risk_if_not_reversed: API calls using the blocked HTTP method fail with 405 Method Not Allowed

reversal_steps: Remove firewall rule blocking the protocol
Or re-enable the protocol in the network device configuration
reversal_basis: Network protocol blocking is enforced via firewall rules (iptables, AWS Security Groups, Azure NSG). Rules are deletable configuration entries.
source_reference: NIST 800-53 SC-7 Boundary Protection | CIS Controls v8 12.2
risk_if_not_reversed: All traffic using the blocked protocol is dropped

reversal_steps: Remove the registry modification block via GPO, EDR policy, or host-based firewall rule
reversal_basis: Registry modification blocking is enforced via GPO (Windows Registry policies), AppLocker, or EDR behavioral rules. These are policy configurations that can be reverted.
source_reference: CIS Benchmarks: Windows Registry hardening | NIST 800-53 CM-7 Least Functionality
risk_if_not_reversed: Legitimate application installers and system tools that require registry writes will fail

reversal_steps: Remove the WAF rule or nginx/apache config blocking the User-Agent pattern
reversal_basis: User-Agent blocking is a WAF or web server configuration rule. It can be added/removed at any time.
risk_if_not_reversed: Legitimate requests from blocked User-Agent string are rejected

reversal_steps: Disable or remove the WAF rule from the rule group
AWS WAF: aws wafv2 update-rule-group
reversal_basis: WAF rules are software configurations. Individual signatures can be enabled/disabled. AWS WAF, Cloudflare, and ModSecurity all support per-rule management.
risk_if_not_reversed: Legitimate traffic matching the WAF pattern is blocked

reversal_steps: Remove CAPTCHA challenge rule from WAF or application layer
reversal_basis: CAPTCHA challenges are WAF or application-level rules that can be toggled. They add a verification step for suspected bot traffic.
risk_if_not_reversed: Legitimate users face CAPTCHA friction on the affected endpoint

reversal_steps: Cleared session data cannot be restored
All users must re-authenticate to create new sessions
reversal_basis: Server-side session stores (Redis, Memcached, database) hold ephemeral session tokens. Clearing forces all users to re-authenticate. Sessions are by definition short-lived and not backed up.
risk_if_not_reversed: All active user sessions terminated — self-resolving on re-authentication

reversal_steps: Re-enable the feature flag in the feature flag management system (LaunchDarkly, Flagsmith, AWS AppConfig)
reversal_basis: Feature flags are runtime configuration toggles. Disabling makes a feature unavailable. Re-enabling restores it. Changes take effect in seconds without deployment.
risk_if_not_reversed: Feature is unavailable to users

reversal_steps: Re-enable the integration in the platform admin settings
Verify integration security before re-enabling after a supply chain incident
reversal_basis: Third-party integrations can be disabled/re-enabled via platform admin settings. Re-enabling after a supply chain incident requires security review of the third-party.
source_reference: NIST 800-53 SA-9 External System Services | ISO 27001 A.5.19
risk_if_not_reversed: Third-party functionality is unavailable to users

reversal_steps: Re-enable the webhook in the application settings or API platform
Verify webhook endpoint is secure before re-enabling after an incident
reversal_basis: Webhooks are configurable integrations that can be enabled/disabled via platform settings. Re-enabling restores event-driven integrations.
risk_if_not_reversed: Event notifications to the webhook consumer stop

reversal_steps: Disable API key requirement in API Gateway settings
Note: Requires security review — removing API authentication is a compliance violation
reversal_basis: API authentication requirements are API Gateway configuration settings. Toggling is possible but disabling violates OWASP API Security API2:2023 (Authentication) and compliance requirements.
source_reference: OWASP API Security API2:2023 — https://owasp.org/API-Security/ | NIST 800-53 IA-3
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling API authentication is a security hardening measure

reversal_steps: Disable bot rules in WAF or Cloudflare bot management settings
reversal_basis: Bot protection rules are WAF/CDN features that can be enabled/disabled via configuration. Disabling removes protection against automated attacks. Security team approval required.
source_reference: Cloudflare Bot Management — https://www.cloudflare.com/products/bot-management/ | OWASP Bot protection
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling bot protection is a hardening measure

reversal_steps: Disable auditd (Linux: systemctl stop auditd) or kernel logging configuration
reversal_basis: Kernel logging (Linux auditd, Windows kernel audit events) is a configuration that can be enabled/disabled. Disabling after an incident removes forensic visibility. Security team approval required.
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling kernel logging is a forensic/audit hardening measure

reversal_steps: Toggle maintenance mode flag off via application admin panel or platform configuration
reversal_basis: Maintenance mode is a feature flag that redirects user traffic to a static maintenance page. Disabling it immediately restores normal application routing.
risk_if_not_reversed: Application is unavailable to all users — SLA/availability impact

reversal_steps: Disable PAM enforcement via the PAM tool administration console
Note: Requires CISO approval — disabling PAM removes a critical security control
reversal_basis: PAM enforcement is a platform-level configuration. Disabling allows privileged access without PAM controls. This is a critical compliance-relevant action requiring CISO-level approval.
source_reference: CIS Controls v8 5.3 / 6.8 | NIST 800-53 AC-6 Least Privilege
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling PAM is a hardening measure

reversal_steps: Disable session recording in PAM tool (CyberArk, BeyondTrust) or monitoring platform
reversal_basis: Session recording is a PAM/monitoring configuration setting. Enabling records privileged sessions. Disabling stops new recordings. Existing recordings are preserved.
source_reference: CIS Controls v8 8.5 | NIST 800-53 AU-12 Audit Record Generation
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — session recording is a hardening/audit measure

reversal_steps: If package was mis-identified, remove it from quarantine in the artifact repository (Artifactory, Nexus, ECR)
reversal_basis: Package quarantine moves a package to an isolated repository space. Restoration requires security team review to confirm the package is safe before restoring to the active feed.
source_reference: CISA: Software Supply Chain Security — https://www.cisa.gov/publication/defending-against-software-supply-chain-attacks | JFrog Xray quarantine
risk_if_not_reversed: Builds requiring the quarantined package will fail

reversal_steps: Remove or raise the rate limit rule in the API Gateway, WAF, or reverse proxy
reversal_basis: Rate limiting is a configurable policy in API Gateways (Kong, AWS API GW, NGINX), WAFs, and reverse proxies. Limits can be adjusted or removed at any time.
source_reference: OWASP: API Security — API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption — https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa4-unrestricted-resource-consumption/
risk_if_not_reversed: Legitimate high-volume API consumers are throttled

reversal_steps: Application restart is self-completing — no reversal needed
reversal_basis: Application restart clears in-memory state and reloads configuration. It is a standard operational procedure with no lasting data change. Sessions may be lost if not using persistent session store.
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — restart is self-completing

reversal_steps: Trigger CI/CD rollback pipeline
Or: git revert <commit-hash> && deploy
Or: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>
reversal_basis: Code deployment rollback re-deploys a prior version. Git revert creates a new commit that undoes the change. Kubernetes rollouts maintain revision history (--revision flag) allowing rollback to any prior version.
source_reference: K8s: Deployment rollback — https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/#rolling-back-a-deployment | Git: git revert — https://git-scm.com/docs/git-revert
risk_if_not_reversed: Potentially vulnerable code version remains deployed

reversal_steps: ⚠️ THIS ACTION REQUIRES HUMAN APPROVAL AND CANNOT BE AUTO-EXECUTED
Re-enable MFA via IdP admin console (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace)
Or re-enforce MFA via IAM policy on the affected account
reversal_basis: Disabling MFA is a security-weakening action that creates vulnerability to credential-based attacks. Per CIS Controls 6.5, MFA is required for externally exposed applications. Disabling it violates PCI-DSS 8.3.10, ISO 27001 A.8.5, and SOC 2 CC6.6. This MUST NOT be auto-executed — always requires human approval. Re-enabling via IdP admin console restores the protection.
source_reference: PCI-DSS v4 8.3.10 | CIS Controls v8 6.5 | ISO 27001:2022 A.8.5 | SOC 2 CC6.6
risk_if_not_reversed: Account is vulnerable to credential stuffing, phishing-based takeover, and unauthorized access without second factor

reversal_steps: Deregistered AMIs cannot be restored
Must create new AMI from a running instance or EBS snapshot
reversal_basis: AWS permanently deregisters AMIs. The underlying EBS snapshots may still exist (unless also deleted), allowing potentially creating a new AMI from them.
risk_if_not_reversed: Cannot launch new instances from this AMI

reversal_steps: Deleted IAM roles cannot be restored
Must recreate role with same name and re-attach all policies
All role-based trust relationships must be re-established
reversal_basis: AWS permanently deletes IAM roles. All attached policies, trust policies, and permission boundaries are lost. Requires full recreation from IaC templates or documented role definitions.
risk_if_not_reversed: Services and principals that assumed this role lose all access

reversal_steps: Deleted IAM users cannot be restored
Must create new user with same username and re-add all group memberships and policies
reversal_basis: AWS permanently deletes IAM users. All associated group memberships, policies, access keys, MFA devices, and SSH keys are destroyed. Must be reconstructed from IaC or manually.
risk_if_not_reversed: User permanently loses all AWS access

reversal_steps: If underlying snapshot preserved: aws ec2 register-image --snapshot-id <snap-id>
reversal_basis: AMI deregistration is permanent. If the backing snapshot was not deleted simultaneously, a new AMI can be created from it — but it gets a new AMI ID.
risk_if_not_reversed: Launch templates and auto-scaling groups referencing this AMI ID will fail

reversal_steps: Run: aws ec2 attach-volume --volume-id <vol-id> --instance-id <inst-id> --device <device>
reversal_basis: EBS volumes persist after detachment. Re-attaching uses the same Volume ID and specifies device name. Volume data is preserved.
risk_if_not_reversed: Instance disk I/O for the detached volume is unavailable

reversal_steps: Run: aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name <role> --policy-arn <arn>
Or: aws iam attach-user-policy --user-name <user> --policy-arn <arn>
reversal_basis: IAM managed policies are reusable — detaching removes the attachment but the policy itself is preserved. Re-attaching with the same ARN restores all permissions.
risk_if_not_reversed: Role/user loses the permissions granted by the policy until reattached

reversal_steps: Run: aws iam update-login-profile --user-name <user> [to restore console access]
Reactivate any deactivated access keys: aws iam update-access-key --status Active
reversal_basis: IAM user disable typically involves deactivating access keys and removing console password. Both are fully reversible — keys can be reactivated (status: Active) and console login re-enabled.
risk_if_not_reversed: User cannot access AWS resources

reversal_steps: Re-enable event source mapping: aws lambda update-event-source-mapping --uuid <uuid> --enabled
reversal_basis: Lambda event source mappings (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams) can be enabled/disabled via UpdateEventSourceMapping. The mapping UUID must be known.
risk_if_not_reversed: Events accumulate in the source queue/stream without processing

reversal_steps: Detach the IAM policy enforcing MFA from the affected role/user/group
Run: aws iam detach-user-policy --policy-arn <mfa-policy-arn>
reversal_basis: MFA enforcement is typically implemented via an IAM policy condition (aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent). Detaching this policy removes the requirement. Reversing MFA requirements needs security team approval per compliance.
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — MFA requirement is a security hardening measure, not a risk

reversal_steps: Run: aws ec2 modify-instance-attribute --instance-id <id> --groups <original-sg-id>
Re-attach original security groups to instance
reversal_basis: EC2 instance isolation works by replacing security groups with a deny-all SG. The original SG IDs must be recorded before isolation. Reversal swaps the SGs back.
risk_if_not_reversed: Instance remains network-isolated and inaccessible to legitimate traffic

reversal_steps: Run: aws iam add-user-to-group --group-name <group> --user-name <user>
reversal_basis: AWS IAM group membership is a simple add/remove operation. Groups persist independently of membership.
risk_if_not_reversed: User loses group-inherited permissions

reversal_steps: Re-create the previous access key using aws iam create-access-key
Update all dependent services to use new key
Deactivate rotated key if needed
reversal_basis: AWS IAM supports multiple active access keys per user. The old key can be re-created (new key ID) or if stored in secrets manager, restored. Rotation is reversible by creating a fresh key.
source_reference: AWS IAM User Guide: Managing access keys — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_access-keys.html
risk_if_not_reversed: Services using the old key will break until updated

reversal_steps: Deleted Lambda functions cannot be restored
Must redeploy from source code repository or CI/CD pipeline
reversal_basis: AWS permanently deletes Lambda functions when deleted. Code, configuration, layers, and event source mappings are destroyed. Must redeploy from code repository.
risk_if_not_reversed: All Lambda-triggered workloads fail permanently

rollback_command: User signs in to Azure AD again
User re-authenticates to get new STS token

reversal_steps: Azure resources once deleted cannot be restored unless recovery options were pre-configured (e.g., soft delete for Key Vault, storage)
reversal_basis: Most Azure resources are permanently deleted. Some (Azure Key Vault, Storage soft-delete) have recovery options if enabled. Must verify soft-delete before assuming irreversibility.
risk_if_not_reversed: Azure resource permanently lost

reversal_steps: GCP Compute instances are permanently deleted
Must create new instance from snapshot if available
reversal_basis: GCP permanently deletes VM instances. Boot disk may be preserved if delete_on_termination=false. Must restore from snapshot or recreate from instance template.
risk_if_not_reversed: VM workload is permanently terminated

reversal_steps: Reapply saved bucket policy: aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket <bucket> --policy file://policy.json
reversal_basis: S3 bucket policies are JSON documents that can be restored if a backup was taken. PutBucketPolicy replaces the current policy entirely.
risk_if_not_reversed: Bucket loses cross-account access and custom permission rules

reversal_steps: aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress/egress --group-id <sg-id> --ip-permissions <original-rule>
reversal_basis: Security group rules are individually addable/removable. Deleted rules can be re-added with the same parameters. Original rule must be documented prior to deletion.
risk_if_not_reversed: Legitimate traffic blocked by missing rule

reversal_steps: Create a new VPC endpoint: aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id <vpc> --service-name <svc> --route-table-ids <rt>
reversal_basis: VPC endpoints are deleted permanently but can be recreated with the same service name. The new endpoint gets a new ID but provides the same private connectivity.
risk_if_not_reversed: Private connectivity to AWS services is disrupted (traffic routes via internet instead)

reversal_steps: az vm start --resource-group <rg> --name <vm-name>
reversal_basis: Azure VM deallocate/stop preserves all VM data and configuration. Starting restores the VM to Running state.
risk_if_not_reversed: VM workload is offline, all network endpoints unreachable

reversal_steps: gcloud services enable <api-name>.googleapis.com --project <project>
reversal_basis: GCP service APIs can be enabled/disabled freely. Re-enabling restores API access immediately.
risk_if_not_reversed: Dependent workloads cannot use the disabled GCP API

reversal_steps: Create new peering request: aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection
Accept from peer: aws ec2 accept-vpc-peering-connection
Re-add routes in both VPCs
reversal_basis: Deleted VPC peering connections cannot be restored. A new peering connection must be established, which requires acceptance from the peer VPC account.
risk_if_not_reversed: Cross-VPC private network traffic is disrupted

reversal_steps: aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket <bucket> --versioning-configuration Status=Suspended
reversal_basis: S3 versioning can be suspended (but not fully disabled once enabled). Suspending stops creation of new versions; existing versions are preserved.
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling versioning is a hardening measure

reversal_steps: Restore original route table associations
Remove deny-all NACLs: aws ec2 replace-network-acl-association
Restore VPC peering routes if needed
reversal_basis: VPC isolation works by modifying route tables and network ACLs to block all traffic. Reversal requires restoring original route table entries and NACL rules. Pre-isolation state must be documented.
risk_if_not_reversed: Entire VPC workload is network-isolated and inaccessible

reversal_steps: Copy object from quarantine bucket back: aws s3 cp s3://quarantine-bucket/<key> s3://original-bucket/<key>
reversal_basis: Object quarantine moves (copy + delete) an S3 object to an isolated quarantine bucket. Reversal copies it back. Requires scan clearance before reversal.
risk_if_not_reversed: Object remains inaccessible from original location

reversal_steps: az role assignment create --assignee <principal> --role '<role>' --scope <scope>
reversal_basis: Azure RBAC role assignments can be re-added with the same principal, role, and scope. Original assignment details must be documented before revocation.
source_reference: Azure RBAC: az role assignment create — https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/role-based-access-control/role-assignments-cli
risk_if_not_reversed: Principal loses access to Azure resources in the specified scope

reversal_steps: gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding <project> --member='<member>' --role='<role>'
reversal_basis: GCP IAM policy bindings are fully reversible. Revoked bindings can be re-added using add-iam-policy-binding with the same member and role.
risk_if_not_reversed: Principal loses all permissions granted by this role

reversal_steps: Restore original bucket ACL: aws s3api put-bucket-acl
Or restore bucket policy: aws s3api put-bucket-policy
reversal_basis: S3 access is controlled via bucket policies and ACLs. Both are replaceable documents. Restoring requires having the original policy/ACL backed up before revocation.
risk_if_not_reversed: Authorized users/services lose access to the bucket

reversal_steps: Delete snapshot if no longer needed: aws ec2 delete-snapshot / gcloud compute snapshots delete / az snapshot delete
reversal_basis: Creating a snapshot is always safe and reversible — the snapshot can be deleted if not needed. The original resource is unaffected.
risk_if_not_reversed: Snapshot stored indefinitely (minor cost impact)

rollback_command: Restore original ingress/egress rules from backup
Recreate bucket and restore from versioning/backup
Object Lock cannot be disabled once enabled on a bucket

reversal_steps: Delete the report from the compliance management system if generated in error
reversal_basis: Compliance reports are documents generated by SIEM/compliance tools. Generating a report is read-only with respect to system configuration. The report itself can be deleted or retracted. Creates no change to the security posture.
source_reference: NIST SP 800-61r2 §3.4 Post-Incident Activity | ISO 27001:2022 A.5.25
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — report generation is a documentation/audit action

rollback_command: Delete incident record from SIEM/case management

reversal_steps: Remove NetworkPolicy or firewall rule blocking registry access
Or restore ImagePullSecret: kubectl create secret docker-registry
reversal_basis: Registry blocking is typically done via NetworkPolicy or firewall rules. These are reversible configuration changes. ImagePullSecrets can be recreated.
source_reference: K8s: Pull images from private registry — https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/pull-image-private-registry/
risk_if_not_reversed: No new images can be pulled — existing pods unaffected, deployments/updates blocked

reversal_steps: kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml (from GitOps repository)
Or recreate: kubectl create configmap <name> --from-file=<config>
reversal_basis: ConfigMaps are deletable Kubernetes resources. Pods using deleted ConfigMaps crash. Re-applying from version control recreates the ConfigMap with all original data.
risk_if_not_reversed: Pods relying on the ConfigMap will fail to start

reversal_steps: Must rebuild from Dockerfile using: docker build -t <image>:<tag>
Or pull from upstream registry if available
reversal_basis: Deleting a container image from a registry is permanent. Images stored only locally or in a registry without replication are lost. Rebuilding requires the Dockerfile and access to base layers.
risk_if_not_reversed: New deployments cannot pull the image

reversal_steps: kubectl apply -f ingress.yaml (from GitOps repository)
reversal_basis: Kubernetes Ingress resources are declarative. Deleting removes external HTTP routing. Re-applying from YAML manifests in version control fully restores it.
risk_if_not_reversed: External HTTP/HTTPS traffic cannot reach the service

reversal_steps: PVC deletion triggers PV reclamation based on reclaimPolicy
If reclaimPolicy=Retain, PV data is preserved and can be re-bound to new PVC
reversal_basis: PVC deletion behavior depends on StorageClass reclaimPolicy. 'Delete' = data gone. 'Retain' = PV data preserved but needs manual re-bind. Always check before deleting.
risk_if_not_reversed: Stateful workload loses persistent storage permanently (if Delete policy)

reversal_steps: Retrieve original secret value from secret manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager)
kubectl create secret generic <name> --from-literal=<key>=<value>
reversal_basis: Kubernetes Secrets are permanently deleted. The secret data must be retrieved from an external secrets manager or backup. Pods consuming the deleted secret will crash.
risk_if_not_reversed: All pods mounting this secret will fail to start

reversal_steps: kubectl apply -f service.yaml (from GitOps repo or backup)
reversal_basis: Kubernetes Services are declarative resources defined in YAML. Deleting a Service removes the DNS name and load balancer endpoint. Re-applying the manifest from version control fully restores it.
risk_if_not_reversed: No network routing to pods — workload inaccessible

reversal_steps: kubectl apply -f mutatingwebhookconfiguration.yaml
Or: kubectl apply -f validatingwebhookconfiguration.yaml
reversal_basis: Admission webhooks are K8s resources that can be deleted and re-created. Disabling removes policy enforcement on resource creation. Re-applying the webhook manifest re-enables it.
risk_if_not_reversed: Security policies (OPA Gatekeeper, Falco) not enforced on new resources

reversal_steps: Remove AppArmor annotation from pod spec and restart
Or set to unconfined: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container>=unconfined
reversal_basis: AppArmor profiles are enforced via pod annotations. The annotation can be changed to 'unconfined' to disable enforcement. Requires security team approval.
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling AppArmor is a hardening measure

reversal_steps: Disable Falco DaemonSet or equivalent: kubectl delete -f falco-daemonset.yaml
reversal_basis: Runtime protection (Falco, Aqua) is deployed as a DaemonSet that can be removed. Disabling must go through security approval as it removes active threat detection.
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling protection is a hardening measure, not a risk

reversal_steps: Update pod spec to remove seccompProfile field and redeploy: kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>
reversal_basis: Seccomp profiles restrict syscalls available to a container. Removing the profile requires updating the pod spec and rolling restart. Approved by security team only.
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — seccomp is a hardening measure

reversal_steps: Delete the deny-all NetworkPolicy: kubectl delete networkpolicy <policy-name> -n <ns>
Or restore original policy: kubectl apply -f original-networkpolicy.yaml
reversal_basis: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is declarative. A deny-all policy added for isolation can be deleted. Original policies must be backed up before isolation or stored in version control.
risk_if_not_reversed: Pod is network-isolated, cannot communicate with other services

reversal_steps: kubectl set resources deployment/<name> --limits=cpu=<original>,memory=<original>
reversal_basis: Kubernetes resource limits (cpu/memory) in pod specs can be updated dynamically. The original resource quotas should be retrieved from GitOps repo or prior kubectl get deployment -o yaml.
risk_if_not_reversed: Container throttled — performance degraded or OOMKilled

reversal_steps: docker unpause <container-id>
reversal_basis: Docker pause uses Linux cgroups freezer subsystem to suspend all processes in the container. Unpausing is immediate and atomic.
source_reference: Docker: docker unpause — https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/commandline/unpause/ | Linux cgroups freezer: https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/cgroup-v1/freezer-subsystem.html
risk_if_not_reversed: Container processes are frozen — inbound requests queue up or timeout

reversal_steps: Container runtime restart: docker run <image>:<tag>
For K8s: kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>
reversal_basis: Containers are ephemeral by design (OCI spec). Removing a container destroys its writable layer state. Image is preserved. Kubernetes Deployments automatically recreate pods via ReplicaSet.
risk_if_not_reversed: Container workload offline until pod is recreated

reversal_steps: kubectl apply -f rolebinding.yaml (from backup)
Or: kubectl create rolebinding <name> --role=<role> --serviceaccount=<ns>:<sa>
reversal_basis: Kubernetes RBAC RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings are declarative resources. Deleting a binding removes the permission. Re-creating with the same spec fully restores access.
risk_if_not_reversed: ServiceAccount/user loses Kubernetes API permissions

reversal_steps: Image scanning is read-only and has no system state change
reversal_basis: Container image scanning (Trivy, Grype, Snyk, ECR scanning) is a passive read operation. It creates scan reports but does not modify the image or system state.
source_reference: Trivy: Container image scanning — https://aquasecurity.github.io/trivy/ | AWS ECR: Image scanning — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/image-scanning.html
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — no system state change

reversal_steps: Scanning running containers is a read-only operation
reversal_basis: Runtime container scanning (Falco, Trivy, Sysdig) passively reads container namespaces and process tables. No system state is modified.
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — read-only operation

reversal_steps: True anonymization is irreversible by design
If pseudonymization was used instead, de-pseudonymize using the mapping table
reversal_basis: GDPR Article 29 WP Opinion 05/2014 on anonymization techniques distinguishes true anonymization (irreversible, not personal data) from pseudonymization (reversible). True anonymization is designed to be irreversible.
source_reference: GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) / Art. 29 WP Op 05/2014 on Anonymisation — https://ec.europa.eu/justice/article-29/documentation/opinion-recommendation/files/2014/wp216_en.pdf
risk_if_not_reversed: Anonymized data cannot be re-identified — any analysis requiring original data is impossible

reversal_steps: Re-run classification scan with corrected rules
Update classification labels in the DLP tool or metadata store
reversal_basis: Data classification is metadata tagging. Classification labels can be updated or reclassified at any time via DLP tools (Macie, Purview, Nightfall). No data modification occurs.
source_reference: Microsoft Purview: Data classification — https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/compliance/data-classification-overview | AWS Macie — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/macie/latest/user/
risk_if_not_reversed: Incorrect classification may lead to over- or under-protection of data

reversal_steps: Contact regulatory body to correct/retract notification if issued in error
Note: Regulatory bodies have formal processes for notification corrections
reversal_basis: GDPR Art. 33 allows notification correction/rectification if initial information proved incorrect. SAR corrections must be submitted formally. Complete retraction is rare and must be agreed with the supervisory authority.
source_reference: GDPR Art. 33 — https://gdpr-info.eu/art-33-gdpr/ | ICO Breach notification guidance
risk_if_not_reversed: Incorrect notification may mislead regulators

reversal_steps: Re-encrypt using the same or new key if data was decrypted for analysis
reversal_basis: Decryption exposes plaintext. If decrypted for authorized investigation, data must be re-encrypted after analysis. Key management must ensure the re-encryption key is stored in KMS.
risk_if_not_reversed: Data remains in plaintext — elevated exposure risk

reversal_steps: Restore from most recent backup
Check recycle bin or trash before initiating full backup restore
reversal_basis: Standard file/record deletion may be recoverable from recycle bin, file system journal, or database transaction log within a short window. Beyond this window, backup restoration is required.
risk_if_not_reversed: Data permanently lost if no backup exists

reversal_steps: Re-enable public sharing in SaaS admin console (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, SharePoint)
reversal_basis: Public sharing is an organizational policy setting in SaaS platforms. Toggling it restricts/allows external link sharing. Reversal requires security team and business justification.
source_reference: ISO 27001:2022 A.5.10 / CIS Controls 3.3 — Configure Data Access Control Lists
risk_if_not_reversed: Users cannot share files externally — business process impact

reversal_steps: Disable access logging via cloud provider settings
Note: Disabling removes audit trail — requires security team approval and may violate compliance requirements
reversal_basis: Access logging is a configurable feature (AWS S3 server access logging, CloudTrail, Azure Monitor). Enabling is a hardening measure. Disabling after an incident removes audit trail evidence.
source_reference: CIS Controls v8 8.2 — Collect Audit Logs | PCI-DSS v4 10.2
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling access logging is a compliance hardening measure

reversal_steps: Disable or modify DLP policy in the DLP management console (Purview, Nightfall, Broadcom DLP)
reversal_basis: DLP policies are configuration-based and can be enabled/disabled at any time. Reversal requires security team approval as disabling DLP removes a GDPR/PCI compliance control.
source_reference: ISO 27001:2022 A.8.12 Data leakage prevention | NIST 800-53 SI-12
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling DLP is a hardening measure

reversal_steps: Disable at-rest encryption via cloud provider or OS settings
Note: Disabling requires security team approval — it removes a compliance control
reversal_basis: Encryption-at-rest can be enabled/disabled on cloud volumes (EBS, Azure Disk, GCP PD). On OS-level (BitLocker, LUKS), disabling requires decryption of the volume which is a lengthy process.
source_reference: NIST SP 800-111 Storage Encryption — https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-111/final | CIS Controls v8 11.3
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling encryption is a hardening/compliance measure

reversal_steps: Disable TLS enforcement on the service
Note: Requires security team approval — removes PCI/HIPAA/NIST compliance control
reversal_basis: TLS enforcement is a server-side configuration. It can be toggled but reversion is a compliance violation for PCI-DSS (4.2), HIPAA §164.312(e), and NIST SC-8. Requires explicit security team approval.
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling TLS is a hardening measure

reversal_steps: Suspend versioning via storage provider settings
Note: Prior versions remain — suspending stops new version creation only
reversal_basis: Storage versioning (S3, GCS, Blob) is a configurable feature. Suspending stops creating new versions; existing versions are preserved. Enabling is always safe.
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling versioning is a data protection hardening measure

reversal_steps: Decrypt using the same key and algorithm: openssl dec -d -aes-256-gcm -in encrypted.bin -out original.dat
reversal_basis: Symmetric encryption (AES-256-GCM per NIST FIPS 197) is reversible using the same key. Key must be preserved and accessible from KMS. Decryption restores original plaintext.
source_reference: NIST FIPS 197 AES — https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/fips/197/final | NIST SP 800-175B Cryptographic Standards — https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-175b/rev-1/final
risk_if_not_reversed: Data remains encrypted — access requires decryption key. Low risk if key is secured.

reversal_steps: Cache cannot be un-invalidated
Application will rebuild cache automatically from source data on next request
reversal_basis: Cache invalidation purges cached data. The application automatically re-populates the cache from the source of truth on the next request. This is a standard cache management operation with no lasting impact.
risk_if_not_reversed: Temporary performance degradation until cache warms up — self-resolving

reversal_steps: Refresh tokens cannot be un-invalidated
User must re-authenticate to get a new refresh token
reversal_basis: OAuth2 refresh tokens are server-side opaque tokens. Revocation via RFC 7009 is permanent. Users simply re-authenticate to receive new access + refresh token pair.
risk_if_not_reversed: User session ended — self-resolving on re-authentication

reversal_steps: Apply inverse transformation using the pseudonymization key/mapping table stored in KMS
reversal_basis: Pseudonymization replaces identifying fields with pseudonyms using a secret mapping (GDPR Rec. 28). Reversal uses the mapping table to restore original identifiers. Requires authorized access to mapping key.
source_reference: GDPR Recital 26, 28 / Art. 4(5) — https://gdpr-info.eu/recitals/no-26/ | ENISA Pseudonymisation — https://www.enisa.europa.eu/publications/pseudonymisation-techniques
risk_if_not_reversed: Data remains pseudonymized — valid for many analytics use cases

reversal_steps: Remove approval workflow from data access request process in the DAG/DLP tool
reversal_basis: Data access approval workflows are configurable DLP/governance tool settings. They can be enabled/disabled by data stewards. Reversal removes friction from data access requests.
source_reference: NIST 800-53 AC-3 Access Enforcement / AC-6 Least Privilege
risk_if_not_reversed: Data access requires manual approval — operational friction but security benefit

reversal_steps: AWS KMS: Re-enable disabled key: aws kms enable-key --key-id <key-id>
Azure Key Vault: Set key to enabled state via portal or CLI
reversal_basis: KMS keys can be disabled (revoked) rather than deleted. Disabled keys cannot be used for crypto operations but can be re-enabled. Deleted keys are irreversible after the key deletion window (7-30 days in AWS).
source_reference: AWS KMS: DisableKey — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/APIReference/API_DisableKey.html | Azure Key Vault: Key operations
risk_if_not_reversed: All data encrypted with this key becomes inaccessible

reversal_steps: Use KMS key versioning to restore prior key version
AWS: aws kms get-key-policy / disable new version
Azure Key Vault: restore previous key version via portal
reversal_basis: Modern KMS solutions (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault) support key versioning. Rotation creates a new key version. Previous versions remain available for decryption of old data. Reverting active encryption key requires re-wrapping data keys.
source_reference: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev5 §5.3 — https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-57-part-1/rev-5/final | AWS KMS: Key rotation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/rotate-keys.html
risk_if_not_reversed: Old services using prior key version may fail to decrypt new data

reversal_steps: Securely deleted data is irrecoverable by design (NIST 800-88)
Original data must have been backed up before deletion to restore
reversal_basis: NIST SP 800-88 Rev.1 defines secure deletion as the rendering of data unrecoverable. Multi-pass overwrite or cryptographic erase (for SSDs, encrypted volumes) ensures data cannot be recovered even with forensic tools.
source_reference: NIST SP 800-88 Rev.1 — Guidelines for Media Sanitization — https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-88r1.pdf
risk_if_not_reversed: Data permanently destroyed — only restoration path is from backup

reversal_steps: Shredded data cannot be recovered at any cost
File must be restored from offline/air-gapped backup if available
reversal_basis: File shredding (e.g., Gutmann 35-pass, DoD 5220.22-M) overwrites the file's disk sectors multiple times. NIST SP 800-88 confirms this renders data unrecoverable with any known technique.
risk_if_not_reversed: Data permanently irrecoverable

reversal_steps: Use document processing tool to remove watermark layer
Or restore from pre-watermark backup
reversal_basis: Digital watermarks can be visible (easily removed via editing) or steganographic (harder). For forensic watermarks, removal may degrade document quality. If original backup exists, restoration is simple.
risk_if_not_reversed: Watermarked document has tracking identifier — minor operational impact

rollback_command: COMMIT; -- or session close releases lock

reversal_steps: Restore from Deleted Items / Trash (typically 30-day retention)
Exchange: Get-RecoverableItems / Restore-RecoverableItems
M365 Defender: eDiscovery Content Search to recover deleted items
reversal_basis: Email deletion in corporate mail systems (Exchange, M365, Google Workspace) has a recoverable deleted items retention period (typically 14–30 days). Items can be recovered via admin tools during retention window.
source_reference: Microsoft 365: Recover deleted email — https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/exchange/recipients/user-mailboxes/deleted-item-recovery | NIST SP 800-61r2 §3.3.4
risk_if_not_reversed: Email permanently lost after retention window — relevant for evidence preservation

reversal_steps: Email recall is the recall itself — no further reversal needed
reversal_basis: Email recall (Microsoft Outlook, Google Workspace) attempts to remove an already-sent email from the recipient's mailbox. Success depends on whether the recipient has already read the email. Only works in same-organization exchanges.
source_reference: Microsoft: Recall a message — https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/recall-or-replace-a-sent-message | CIS Controls v8 9.2
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — recall is a remediation action itself

rollback_command: Remove USB device class block policy

reversal_steps: Re-enable Autorun via GPO: Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → Windows Components → AutoPlay Policies
reversal_basis: Windows Autorun is controlled by GPO and Registry settings. Disabling it prevents automatic execution of media content (a recommended security hardening per CIS). Re-enabling via GPO is straightforward.
source_reference: CIS Benchmarks: Windows Autorun disable — Control 10.2 | Microsoft: Autorun Disable — https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/topic/how-to-disable-the-autorun-functionality-in-windows
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — disabling Autorun is a security hardening measure

reversal_steps: Re-enable USB storage via GPO: Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → System → Removable Storage Access
Or via EDR policy (CrowdStrike USB device control)
reversal_basis: USB storage restriction is enforced via Windows Group Policy or EDR device control policies. Disabling USB blocks removable media. Re-enabling via GPO or EDR policy console restores USB access. Business justification required for reversal (e.g., authorized data transfer).
source_reference: CIS Controls v8 10.3 — Disable Autorun and Autoplay for Removable Media | NIST 800-53 MP-7 Media Use
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — disabling USB is a security hardening measure preventing data exfiltration

rollback_command: Start the process again via service manager or manual invocation
Move {file} from quarantine vault back to original path

reversal_steps: If file was restored in error, delete the restored copy or overwrite with correct version
reversal_basis: File restoration from backup overwrites the current file with a backup version. The restoration itself can be reversed by deleting the restored file or overwriting it with the correct version.
source_reference: NIST SP 800-61r2 §3.3.4 Recovery | CIS Controls v8 11.1
risk_if_not_reversed: Restored file may be an older version that overwrote newer legitimate changes

reversal_steps: Restore a different registry backup if wrong version was applied
regedit: File → Import → [correct backup .reg file]
reversal_basis: Windows Registry restoration from backup overwrites current registry keys. Applying a different backup or manually reverting specific keys can undo an incorrect restoration. Multiple backup points should exist.
source_reference: Microsoft: Back up and restore the registry — https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/topic/how-to-back-up-and-restore-the-registry-in-windows | NIST 800-53 CP-10
risk_if_not_reversed: Incorrect registry state may cause application or OS instability

rollback_command: Take snapshot of current state then restore to desired snapshot

reversal_steps: Re-apply the update/patch: Windows: Run Windows Update again | Linux: apt install <package>=<version> | WSUS: re-push update
reversal_steps_note: Reapplying a security patch requires security team confirmation that the patch is safe
reversal_basis: System update rollback reverts OS or application patches to prior versions. Windows Restore Points, WSUS rollback, and package downgrade (apt/yum) support this. Re-applying the update required if the rollback was done in error.
source_reference: NIST 800-53 CM-3 Configuration Change Control | CIS Controls v8 7.3
risk_if_not_reversed: System remains on older, potentially vulnerable version

rollback_command: Recreate task via schtasks or cron

reversal_steps: Release host from containment via EDR console (CrowdStrike: Lift Containment | SentinelOne: Network Control → Off | Defender: Remove isolation)
reversal_basis: EDR host containment (network isolation) is a feature that can be enabled/disabled from the EDR management console. Lifting containment restores full network connectivity to the host.
risk_if_not_reversed: Host remains network-isolated — cannot communicate with other systems

reversal_steps: EDR remediation (quarantine + kill process) is permanent for the specific threat artifact
If incorrect: restore affected files from backup or quarantine store
reversal_basis: EDR remediation kills malicious processes and quarantines threat artifacts. Quarantined files can be restored from the EDR quarantine store if mis-classified. Killed processes must be re-started manually.
source_reference: NIST SP 800-61r2 §3.3.3 Eradication | CrowdStrike: Quarantine — https://www.crowdstrike.com/
risk_if_not_reversed: If false positive: legitimate process killed, legitimate file quarantined

rollback_command: Restore from full endpoint backup via MDM or backup agent
Restore from a newer backup snapshot
git checkout {commit} -- {file} or restore from backup

reversal_steps: Malware analysis is read-only — no system state change
reversal_basis: Static and dynamic malware analysis is performed in an isolated sandbox. No production system state is modified. Analysis produces reports but does not alter the environment.
source_reference: NIST SP 800-61r2 §3.2 Detection and Analysis — https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-61r2.pdf | CAPA / YARA analysis tools
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — analysis is read-only

reversal_steps: Hash calculation is read-only — no file modification
reversal_basis: File hashing (MD5, SHA-256, SHA-512) reads file contents without modifying them. It is a standard integrity verification technique per NIST SP 800-101 and forensic best practice (RFC 3227).
source_reference: RFC 3227 | NIST SP 800-101 Rev1 — Guidelines on Mobile Device Forensics | NIST FIPS 202 SHA standard
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — read-only operation

reversal_steps: EDR forensics collection is a read-only operation
reversal_basis: EDR forensics (CrowdStrike RTR, SentinelOne Remote Script, Defender for Endpoint) collects process trees, network connections, and file metadata. Read-only by design — no system state modification.
source_reference: NIST SP 800-86 Guide to Integrating Forensics — https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-86/final | CrowdStrike RTR
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — forensic collection is read-only

reversal_steps: Stopping packet capture terminates the collection — no reversal needed
reversal_basis: Network packet capture (tcpdump, Wireshark, AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring) is passive. It copies packets without affecting the original traffic flow. PCAP collection is standard digital forensics per RFC 3227.
source_reference: RFC 3227: Guidelines for Evidence Collection — https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3227 | NIST SP 800-86
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — packet capture is read-only

reversal_steps: Delete the process dump file after analysis is complete
Dump file may contain sensitive data — handle per data retention policy
reversal_basis: Process memory dumps are created by reading process memory space (Task Manager, ProcDump, WinPmem). The process continues running unless explicitly killed. The dump file is an artifact that can be deleted after analysis.
risk_if_not_reversed: Dump file occupies disk space — delete after analysis

reversal_steps: Volatile data collection is read-only — no system modification
reversal_basis: Volatile data collection (running processes, network connections, memory contents, login sessions) is read-only per the Order of Volatility (RFC 3227). Collection must happen before any system changes.
source_reference: RFC 3227 Order of Volatility — https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3227 | NIST SP 800-86
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — read-only collection

reversal_steps: Event correlation is an analysis operation — no system state change
reversal_basis: Event correlation (SIEM correlation rules, AI-based correlation) processes log data to identify related events. It is a pure analysis operation with no effect on source systems or logs.
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — read-only analysis

reversal_steps: Delete the forensic snapshot after analysis: aws ec2 delete-snapshot / gcloud compute snapshots delete
reversal_basis: Forensic snapshots (disk images, VM snapshots) preserve system state at a point in time. The original system is unaffected. Snapshots can be deleted after the investigation.
source_reference: NIST SP 800-86 §5.2 Disk Forensics | AWS EC2: CreateSnapshot
risk_if_not_reversed: Snapshot consumes storage (minor cost impact)

reversal_steps: Delete the snapshot when no longer needed: aws ec2 delete-snapshot, gcloud compute snapshots delete, az snapshot delete
reversal_basis: System/volume snapshots are point-in-time copies. Creating a snapshot is always safe (non-destructive). The original resource is unaffected.
risk_if_not_reversed: Snapshot stored indefinitely (minor cost impact)

reversal_steps: IOC extraction is read-only analysis
reversal_basis: IOC extraction (IPs, domains, hashes, URLs from malware/logs) is a pure analysis and data transformation operation. No system state is modified. STIX/TAXII are data format standards for IOC exchange.
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — read-only analysis

reversal_steps: Timeline analysis is read-only — no system modification
reversal_basis: Timeline analysis reconstructs event sequences from logs and filesystem metadata (MAC timestamps). Tools like Plaso/log2timeline process data read-only.
source_reference: NIST SP 800-86 §5.5 Timeline Analysis | Plaso — https://plaso.readthedocs.io/
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — read-only analysis

reversal_steps: Restore from an alternative (newer) snapshot if the wrong point-in-time was restored
reversal_basis: Snapshot restoration replaces current system state with a prior state. Data created after the snapshot timestamp is lost. Reversal requires a newer snapshot or backup. Per NIST 800-61r2 §3.3.4, always verify snapshot integrity before restore.
risk_if_not_reversed: System remains at prior state — data changes after the snapshot are lost

rollback_command: Recreate account from AD backup or manual provisioning
Remove MFA policy from user account
Set pwdLastSet=0 in AD or remove shadow file age
All users re-authenticate per normal session policy
net user {username} /active:yes OR AD attribute unlock
Generate new API token for the application
User re-authenticates to receive new TGT
Re-authorize the application to get new OAuth token
Restore permissions from RBAC backup snapshot
Restore prior service account key if not yet expired

reversal_steps: MySQL: ALTER USER '<user>'@'<host>' ACCOUNT UNLOCK;
MSSQL: ALTER LOGIN <login> ENABLE;
Postgres: ALTER ROLE <role> LOGIN;
reversal_basis: Database login accounts can be locked/unlocked without deleting them. The account and all its permissions survive the lock. Unlocking is a SQL statement.
source_reference: MySQL: ALTER USER — https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.0/en/alter-user.html | MSSQL: ALTER LOGIN — https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/t-sql/statements/alter-login-transact-sql
risk_if_not_reversed: Application database connections fail authentication

reversal_steps: Re-enable LDAP bind account in Active Directory or LDAP directory
Or restore the bind password and update application configs
reversal_basis: LDAP bind accounts are used by applications for directory queries. Disabling (or rotating the password) breaks application authentication. Re-enabling or updating the password restores LDAP connectivity.
risk_if_not_reversed: Applications using this LDAP bind account cannot authenticate users

reversal_steps: Remove the access grant via IAM, RBAC, or file permission settings
reversal_basis: Access grants are additive permission entries. Revoking removes the entry. Per NIST AC-2, access should be granted on a least-privilege basis and promptly revoked when no longer needed.
source_reference: NIST 800-53 AC-2 Account Management / AC-6 Least Privilege
risk_if_not_reversed: Granted access remains active — verify it was legitimately required

reversal_steps: Add the user/device back to the group via IAM, AD, or application console
reversal_basis: Group membership is a simple add/remove operation in all IAM systems. Restoring membership re-grants all group-derived permissions.
risk_if_not_reversed: User loses group-derived permissions

reversal_steps: Revert to standing access by disabling JIT policy in PAM tool (CyberArk, BeyondTrust, AWS IAM Identity Center)
reversal_basis: JIT access is implemented via PAM tools that require approval workflows for sensitive access. Reverting to standing access requires disabling the JIT policy and approving restoration. Per CIS Controls 6.5 principle of least privilege.
source_reference: CIS Controls v8 Control 6 — https://www.cisecurity.org/controls/v8/ | CyberArk JIT — https://docs.cyberark.com/Product-Doc/OnlineHelp/PAS/Latest/en/Content/PASIMP/jit-access.htm
risk_if_not_reversed: Administrative access requires per-request approval (operational slowdown)

reversal_steps: Remove step-up authentication policy or session extension grant
reversal_basis: Step-up MFA requirements are policy configurations on the IdP/application session. Removing the policy reverts to standard session lifetime. Short-lived security measure by design.
risk_if_not_reversed: Users repeatedly prompted for MFA (operational friction)

reversal_steps: Remove the 'must change password at next logon' flag via IAM/AD admin portal
reversal_basis: Password change requirements are flags on user accounts (e.g., AD pwdLastSet=0 or IAM 'PasswordResetRequired'). These flags can be cleared by an admin if the requirement was set in error. Reversing needs security team approval.
source_reference: Microsoft AD: pwdLastSet attribute — https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/adschema/a-pwdlastset | AWS IAM: update-login-profile — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/reference/iam/update-login-profile.html
risk_if_not_reversed: User must change password on next login (minor operational friction)

reversal_steps: Active sessions are terminated permanently
Users must re-authenticate to create new sessions
reversal_basis: Session revocation forces all active tokens to expire immediately. Re-authentication creates brand new sessions. This is intentional isolation behavior per NIST SP 800-61r2 containment guidance.
source_reference: NIST SP 800-61r2 §3.3.1 Containment — https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-61r2.pdf | OWASP: Session revocation — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
risk_if_not_reversed: All legitimate users temporarily logged out — resolved on re-auth within minutes

reversal_steps: Generate a replacement API key via the respective service
Update all dependent integrations with the new key
reversal_basis: API keys are single-use secrets — once revoked they cannot be restored. Best practice per NIST SP 800-63B is immediate revocation of compromised credentials, followed by issuing a new key.
risk_if_not_reversed: All services using the revoked API key receive 401/403 errors until updated

reversal_steps: Application must re-authenticate via OAuth2 client credentials flow to get a new token
reversal_basis: OAuth2 application tokens (client credentials flow) cannot be un-revoked. The application re-authenticates with client_id/client_secret to get a new access token.
source_reference: RFC 6749 OAuth2 §4.4 — https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc6749 | RFC 7009 Token Revocation — https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7009
risk_if_not_reversed: Application API calls fail — resolved when application re-authenticates

reversal_steps: Generate a new certificate signing request (CSR)
Submit to CA for signing
Deploy new certificate to affected services
reversal_basis: Digital certificate revocation is permanent (CRL/OCSP). Per RFC 5280, revoked certificates remain in the CRL indefinitely. A new certificate with a new serial number must be issued.
source_reference: RFC 5280 §3.3 — https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5280 | NIST SP 800-57 Key Management — https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-57-part-1/rev-5/final
risk_if_not_reversed: TLS/mTLS connections using the revoked certificate are rejected

reversal_steps: Re-grant data access through DBAC/DAC policy
Update SaaS platform sharing settings or IAM data policies
reversal_basis: Data access controls (SharePoint permissions, Google Drive ACLs, database role grants) are configurable. Revoking removes access entries. Re-granting restores them. Business justification required for reversal.
risk_if_not_reversed: Users/services cannot access required data resources

reversal_steps: MySQL/Postgres: GRANT <privs> ON <db>.* TO '<user>'@'<host>';
MSSQL: GRANT <permission> ON <object> TO <principal>;
reversal_basis: SQL GRANT/REVOKE are standard DML commands. REVOKE removes a privilege; GRANT restores it. Original grant details must be known (what was revoked).
risk_if_not_reversed: Application/user cannot perform previously authorized database operations

reversal_steps: Generate replacement token in the third-party integration settings
Update integration configuration with new token
reversal_basis: Integration tokens (Slack, GitHub, Jira, etc.) are single-use secrets. Once revoked, they cannot be restored. New tokens must be generated and distributed to dependent systems.
source_reference: GitHub: Revoking tokens — https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/reviewing-your-authorized-oauth-apps | OWASP API Security Top 10
risk_if_not_reversed: Third-party integration broken until new token is configured

reversal_steps: JWTs are self-contained and cannot be un-revoked
User must log in again to receive a new JWT
reversal_basis: JWTs are stateless by design (RFC 7519). Revocation requires server-side token blocklisting. The specific token cannot be 'un-revoked'; the user obtains a new token on re-authentication.
source_reference: RFC 7519 JWT — https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc7519 | OWASP: JWT Security — https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/JSON_Web_Token_for_Java_Cheat_Sheet.html
risk_if_not_reversed: User is logged out from all sessions — resolved on re-authentication

reversal_steps: User must re-enroll TOTP/FIDO2 device through account security portal
Admin may need to initiate MFA reset
reversal_basis: MFA device (TOTP, FIDO2) deregistration is reversible by re-enrollment. Per NIST SP 800-63B, re-enrollment must use identity proofing. A new device is enrolled, not the old one restored.
risk_if_not_reversed: User cannot complete MFA challenge and is locked out until re-enrolled

reversal_steps: Re-assign the role to the user/group via IAM, AD, or application RBAC console
reversal_basis: Role assignment in RBAC systems is additive/removable. Revoking a role removes permissions granted by that role. Re-assigning it restores them. Per AC-6 (Least Privilege), a re-assignment should be re-justified.
risk_if_not_reversed: User loses all permissions granted by the revoked role

reversal_steps: SAML assertions are one-time use (NotOnOrAfter constraint)
User must re-authenticate through IdP to receive a new assertion
reversal_basis: SAML 2.0 assertions are short-lived (typically 5 minutes) per the spec. Revoking forces early expiry. New assertions are generated on IdP re-authentication.
risk_if_not_reversed: User is logged out from SP — resolved on next IdP authentication

reversal_steps: Re-enable service account credentials in the relevant platform
Azure: Enable Service Principal. GCP: enable SA. K8s: restore ServiceAccount
reversal_basis: Service account revocation disables the service identity. All services running under it fail authentication. Re-enabling the account and distributing new credentials restores operation.
risk_if_not_reversed: All services running as this SA lose authentication access

reversal_steps: Generate a new share link in the sharing application (Google Drive, SharePoint, OneDrive)
reversal_basis: Share link revocation invalidates the specific URL token. A new share link can be generated with the same permissions. The new link gets a different URL token.
source_reference: Google Drive: Sharing files — https://support.google.com/drive/answer/2494822 | Microsoft SharePoint: Sharing links — https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/share-sharepoint-files-or-folders
risk_if_not_reversed: External recipients with the revoked link lose access

reversal_steps: Old credentials are permanently deactivated after rotation
Update all dependent services with new credential values from secrets manager
reversal_basis: Service credential rotation generates new secrets and deactivates old ones. Per NIST SP 800-63B and SOC 2 CC6.7, this is a planned security action. All consumers must be updated from the secrets manager.
source_reference: NIST SP 800-63B §5.2.7 | AWS Secrets Manager: Rotation — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/rotating-secrets.html
risk_if_not_reversed: Services with old credentials receive authentication failures until updated

reversal_steps: Old secret cannot be restored after rotation
Update all consumers of the secret with the new value
reversal_basis: API secret rotation generates a new cryptographic secret. The old secret is deactivated. New secret must be distributed to all consumers. Rotation is a standard security hygiene procedure per NIST SP 800-63B.
source_reference: NIST SP 800-63B §5.2.7 — https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html | SOC 2 CC6.7 Credential Management
risk_if_not_reversed: Services using the old secret receive authentication failures

reversal_steps: Re-enable account via IAM/AD console
AWS: aws iam update-login-profile / update-access-key --status Active
AD: Enable-ADAccount -Identity <user>
reversal_basis: Account suspension preserves all account attributes while blocking access. Re-enabling is a single administrative action. Per NIST SP 800-61r2, account suspension is a standard containment action during incident investigation.
risk_if_not_reversed: User cannot access any systems

reversal_steps: Close or delete the ticket in the ITSM system if created in error
reversal_basis: Incident tickets in ITSM systems (ServiceNow, Jira, PagerDuty) can be closed or deleted by authorized administrators. Creating a ticket has no impact on system state.
source_reference: CIS Controls v8 17.3 — Establish enterprise process for incident management
risk_if_not_reversed: Unnecessary open ticket in ITSM system

reversal_steps: Escalation is a communication action — no system state change
reversal_basis: Escalation notifies management about the incident. It is a communication action that creates no system state change. Per NIST SP 800-61r2, escalation is a standard part of incident coordination.
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — communication action

reversal_steps: Notification is a communication action — no system state change
reversal_basis: Notifying the incident commander is a paging/alerting action. It creates a notification event but does not modify any system state. Standard practice per NIST SP 800-61r2 and ICS (Incident Command System).
source_reference: NIST SP 800-61r2 §3.2.7 | ICS (Incident Command System) — FEMA IS-100.C
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — communication action

reversal_steps: ⚠️ THIS ACTION REQUIRES HUMAN APPROVAL AND CANNOT BE AUTO-EXECUTED
Check SIEM long-term storage or WORM storage for log backup
Restore from centralized log archive (Splunk, Elastic, Glacier, Cloudwatch Logs)
reversal_basis: Audit log deletion is a high-risk, potentially irreversible action that undermines forensic investigation capability and triggers compliance violations (PCI 10.5.1, HIPAA §164.312(b), NIST AU-9). Deleted logs may be recoverable from SIEM/WORM archives only if pre-configured. This action MUST NEVER be auto-executed — always routes to L1/L2 analyst queue for manual approval regardless of context.
source_reference: PCI-DSS v4 10.5.1 | NIST 800-53 AU-9 (Protection of Audit Information) | HIPAA §164.312(b) | ISO 27001 A.8.15 — https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-53/rev-5/final
risk_if_not_reversed: Permanent loss of forensic evidence — potential compliance violation across all frameworks (PCI, HIPAA, GDPR, NIST, ISO 27001). Chain of custody broken.

reversal_steps: ⚠️ Disabling audit logging requires security team approval — it removes compliance controls
Linux: systemctl stop auditd
AWS: Disable CloudTrail trail
Azure: Disable diagnostic settings
reversal_basis: Audit logging is enabled via OS/cloud configuration (auditd, CloudTrail, Azure Monitor). Enabling is a hardening measure that creates no data loss risk. Disabling after the fact is a compliance violation for PCI-DSS (10.2), HIPAA (§164.312(b)), and NIST 800-53 (AU-12). Disabling requires explicit security team authorization.
source_reference: PCI-DSS v4 10.2 | HIPAA §164.312(b) | NIST 800-53 AU-12 Audit Record Generation | CIS Controls v8 8.1
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling audit logging is a compliance hardening measure

reversal_steps: Remove DLP or firewall rule blocking the identified exfiltration path
reversal_basis: Data exfiltration blocking is done via DLP policies and firewall rules targeting specific destinations or data patterns. These are configurable policies that can be removed after the threat is remediated.
source_reference: NIST 800-53 SI-12 / AC-4 Information Flow Enforcement | ISO 27001 A.8.12
risk_if_not_reversed: Legitimate data transfers on the blocked path continue to be blocked

rollback_command: Remove DNS sinkhole or firewall rule for {domain}

reversal_steps: Remove the domain from the blocked senders list in the email gateway (Proofpoint, Mimecast, M365 Defender)
reversal_basis: Email domain blocking is a mail gateway policy setting. Adding/removing domains from block lists is a standard administrative operation.
source_reference: Microsoft 365 Defender: Block senders — https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/security/office-365-security/ | CIS Controls v8 9.2
risk_if_not_reversed: Legitimate emails from the blocked domain are quarantined

reversal_steps: Remove the sensor appliance or virtual sensor from the network segment
reversal_basis: Network sensors (IDS/IPS probes, NDR sensors) are passive or inline monitoring devices. Removing a passive sensor has no impact on traffic. Removing an inline sensor requires reverting the network path change.
source_reference: NIST 800-53 SI-4 System Monitoring | CIS Controls v8 8.9
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — deploying a sensor is a monitoring hardening measure

reversal_steps: Disable NetFlow/IPFIX export on the network device interface
reversal_basis: NetFlow is a passive traffic metadata export feature. Enabling it adds monitoring traffic without affecting network connectivity. Disabling stops metadata export.
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling NetFlow is a monitoring hardening measure

reversal_steps: Remove the port mirror/SPAN configuration from the switch or virtual switch
reversal_basis: Network taps (physical) and SPAN sessions (virtual) are additive monitoring configurations. Removing the SPAN session removes traffic duplication without affecting original traffic.
source_reference: NIST 800-53 AU-12 Audit Record Generation | CIS Controls v8 8.2
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling a network tap is a monitoring hardening measure

rollback_command: Disable SSL inspection policy on proxy/firewall
Restore original VLAN or security group configuration

reversal_steps: Delete the SPAN session or traffic mirror session
AWS: aws ec2 delete-traffic-mirror-session
reversal_basis: Traffic mirroring creates duplicate copies of packets and sends them to a monitoring destination. The original traffic is unaffected. Removing the mirror session stops the duplication.
source_reference: AWS VPC Traffic Mirroring — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/mirroring/ | NIST 800-53 SI-4
risk_if_not_reversed: N/A — enabling traffic mirroring is a forensic monitoring measure

rollback_command: Restore firewall ruleset from backup snapshot
Switch port back to original VLAN

reversal_steps: Flush DNS cache: Windows: ipconfig /flushdns | Linux: systemd-resolve --flush-caches | AWS Route53: Wait for TTL expiry
reversal_basis: DNS cache poisoning as a defensive measure (redirecting malicious domain to sinkhole) can be reversed by flushing the DNS cache. TTL-based expiry is automatic. Defensive DNS poisoning is a valid threat response per CISA guidance.
source_reference: CISA: DNS Sinkholing — https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories | NIST 800-53 SC-20 Secure Name/Address Resolution
risk_if_not_reversed: Redirected domain continues to go to sinkhole until DNS cache is flushed

reversal_steps: Unblocking an IP is itself the reversal of block_ip
If re-blocking needed: reinstate the firewall rule
reversal_basis: IP unblocking removes a deny rule from the firewall or security group. It is a low-complexity configuration change that can be immediately reverted if re-blocking is needed.
risk_if_not_reversed: Previously blocked IP regains network access

reversal_steps: Restore prior rule set from backup: iptables-restore < iptables-backup.txt
Or revert to prior Security Group version in cloud console
reversal_basis: Firewall rules are configuration entries that can be added/removed. iptables, AWS Security Groups, and Azure NSG all support rule management. Prior rule sets should be exported before modification.
source_reference: NIST 800-53 SC-7 Boundary Protection | CIS Controls v8 12.1
risk_if_not_reversed: Network access may be different from the intended baseline security posture

rollback_command: Send follow-up clarification to affected users
File correction/retraction with DPA if notification was in error
Send follow-up message noting false positive
Contact ISAC to retract IOC if submitted in error
Revert EDR/AV signature database to previous version
